kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A retailer's new demand forecast is more accurate than store managers' own estimates in back-testing, yet six weeks after launch managers override it for 70% of orders. Head office proposes removing the override function. Managers say the forecast 'doesn't know about local events'. The retailer's chief executive was profiled in a magazine last week. What should the analyst do first?
why: Overriding at this rate signals that the people expected to use the forecast do not trust it, and they have given a specific reason. Understanding that reason comes first: it may expose a real gap in the model or a concern that can be addressed. Forcing compliance or repeating accuracy figures does neither.

options.text: Find out why managers override, including the local factors the forecast may be missing.
options.verdict: The managers have named a specific weakness, and it needs examining before anything is imposed.

options.text: Send managers the back-testing results, so that they can see the forecast's accuracy.
options.verdict: Average accuracy does not answer a concern about particular local circumstances.

options.text: Retrain the forecast on a longer history, so that its accuracy improves further.
options.verdict: More history will not supply information about local events the model never sees.

options.text: Remove the override function, since back-testing shows the forecast is more accurate.
options.verdict: Forcing use ignores a possibly valid objection and hardens resistance.

task: Document and Communicate Findings from Completed Analysis
trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: An analysis of loan-officer decisions at a bank finds that one branch approves 15% fewer applications from a particular suburb. The sample for that suburb is 48 applications. The retail head wants the finding in tomorrow's board pack under the heading 'Branch bias identified'. The bank's sponsorship of a cricket team was announced today. How should the analyst document the finding?
why: The difference is worth attention, but 48 applications is thin support for a conclusion as serious as bias. Responsible reporting states what was observed, how strong the evidence is and what should happen next. Overstating it, burying it or hiding the sample size each misrepresent the evidence.

options.text: Report the approval rate without the sample size, to keep the board pack concise.
options.verdict: Without the sample size the board cannot judge how much weight the figure deserves.

options.text: Omit it from the board pack, since a sample of 48 cannot support any reportable finding.
options.verdict: A possible fairness issue should be surfaced with caveats, not suppressed.

options.text: Report it as a preliminary signal with the small sample stated, and recommend further review.
options.verdict: This gives the board the observation and its weight, and proposes how to firm it up.

options.text: Report it under the proposed heading, since the board should see evidence of bias promptly.
options.verdict: The heading asserts a conclusion that 48 applications cannot carry.

trap: Choosing the most thorough option when the scenario constrains time or access
stem: A tourism board wants to know what share of visitors to a coastal region are day-trippers rather than overnight stayers, to guide a marketing budget decision next month. National visitor survey data covering the region is published quarterly at no cost. A consultancy proposes a custom intercept survey costing $80,000 and taking five months. The board chair prefers 'our own data'. What should the analyst plan?
why: The decision is next month and an existing source already covers the question. Planning collection means checking whether available data is good enough for the decision before paying for new data. A five-month survey cannot inform a decision due in four weeks, however well it is designed.

options.text: Combine vendor mobile-location data with accommodation bookings to model visitor types.
options.verdict: This is more elaborate than the question requires and cannot be assembled in the time.

options.text: Follow the chair's preference and design an in-house survey that board staff can administer.
options.verdict: A preference for owning the data does not make a new survey timely or necessary.

options.text: Commission the intercept survey, because data collected for the purpose is more accurate.
options.verdict: Purpose-built data may be better, but it arrives four months after the decision.

options.text: Use the published survey data first and assess whether it answers the question well enough.
options.verdict: An existing free source covers the region, and it is available before the decision is due.

trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A subscription meal-kit company has framed its problem: customers who pause deliveries often never resume. The decision to be supported is which paused customers should receive a win-back offer costing $15 each. The marketing lead proposes the research question 'What do our customers think of our brand?'. A new packaging supplier starts next month. Which research question best fits the decision?
why: The decision is who gets a $15 offer, so the useful question is whose behaviour the offer changes. Customers who would resume anyway cost $15 for nothing, which is why predicting resumption alone answers a neighbouring question. Brand opinion and pause counts do not discriminate between customers at all.

options.text: How many customers paused deliveries in each of the last twelve months?
options.verdict: This describes the size of the problem but gives no basis for choosing who receives an offer.

options.text: Which paused customers are most likely to resume their deliveries anyway?
options.verdict: These are the customers on whom the $15 would be wasted, so this answers a different question.

options.text: Which paused customers are likely to resume only if they receive an offer?
options.verdict: The offer creates value only where it changes behaviour, and this question targets exactly those customers.

options.text: What do customers who have paused deliveries think of the brand overall?
options.verdict: Brand opinion does not indicate which individual customers should be sent the offer.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: An analyst has collected twelve months of sales transactions for a pricing study. Total revenue in the extract is 6% lower than the audited finance report for the same period. The pricing manager says 6% is 'close enough' and wants results by month end. The company recently changed its email provider. What should the analyst do?
why: A 6% shortfall is unlikely to be spread evenly. If it reflects a missing channel, region or period, pricing conclusions drawn from the extract would be biased in a way nobody could see. Finding the cause is the validation step; scaling, footnoting or substituting totals each leave the cause unknown.

options.text: Replace the extract with the finance report totals, since audited figures are more reliable.
options.verdict: Aggregate totals cannot support a pricing study that needs transaction-level detail.

options.text: Investigate the cause of the 6% gap before the extract is used for the pricing analysis.
options.verdict: The gap may be a whole channel or period, and the analysis is unsafe until that is known.

options.text: Proceed with the analysis and note the 6% difference as a limitation in the final report.
options.verdict: A footnote does not help if the missing revenue is concentrated where prices differ.

options.text: Scale all transaction values up by 6% so that the extract's total matches the finance report.
options.verdict: Scaling forces the totals to agree while hiding whatever is missing from the extract.

trap: Treating correlation as causation
stem: Exploring store data for a pharmacy chain, the analyst finds that stores with more staff per shift have higher sales, with a correlation of 0.7. The operations director concludes that adding staff will lift sales and asks for a hiring budget. Store floor area is also in the data set. The chain's uniforms were redesigned this year. What should the analyst point out?
why: A correlation shows the two move together, not that one produces the other. Bigger or busier stores plausibly have both more staff and more sales, and floor area in the data offers a way to check. Until that is examined, a hiring budget rests on an untested causal claim.

options.text: The uniform redesign coincided with the data period and may explain the higher sales.
options.verdict: The redesign applied across the chain, so it cannot explain differences between stores.

options.text: A correlation of 0.7 is too weak to support any conclusion about staffing and sales.
options.verdict: A value of 0.7 is a strong association; the issue is what it means, not its size.

options.text: The correlation shows that sales cause staffing, so the hiring budget is unnecessary.
options.verdict: Reversing the direction is as unsupported as the director's original claim.

options.text: Larger or busier stores may drive both staffing and sales, so the link may not be causal.
options.verdict: A third factor such as store size could explain both, and the data allows that to be checked.

trap: Mistaking statistical significance for business significance
stem: An online retailer tested a new checkout button colour on two million visitors, with the result below. The marketing lead wants to announce a 'statistically proven winner'. Making the change requires a two-week development freeze costing about $90,000. The retailer's warehouse lease is up for renewal. What insight should the analyst draw?

exhibit.title: Checkout button test
exhibit.note: Difference 0.06 percentage points, p = 0.02. Estimated annual profit gain if rolled out: $12,000.

why: With a million visitors per group, even a tiny difference is detectable, so the result is unlikely to be chance. Whether it matters is a separate question, and a $12,000 annual gain against a $90,000 cost says it would take years to pay for itself. Statistical significance is not business significance.

options.text: The effect is real but small, and its value does not cover the cost of implementing it.
options.verdict: The test detects a genuine difference, but one worth less than it costs to deliver.

options.text: The effect is too small to be real, so the result should be treated as random noise.
options.verdict: A p-value of 0.02 on two million visitors indicates a real, if small, difference.

options.text: The effect is statistically proven, so the new button should be rolled out to all visitors.
options.verdict: Significance shows the difference is unlikely to be chance, not that it is worth acting on.

options.text: The effect is inconclusive, so the test should be rerun on a larger number of visitors.
options.verdict: The test is already conclusive; more visitors would only confirm the same small effect.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: Preparing survey data on commuter satisfaction, the analyst finds the income question blank for 22% of respondents, and blanks are far more common among respondents over 65. The planned analysis compares satisfaction across income bands. A colleague suggests filling the blanks with the overall median income. The survey used a prize draw as an incentive. What is the main concern with that suggestion?
why: The missing answers are concentrated in one group, so they are not random. Giving them all the median pushes a large block of older respondents into a single middle band, and that band's satisfaction then partly reflects age, not income. The comparison the analysis exists to make would be distorted.

options.text: It would breach the terms of the prize draw under which respondents gave their answers.
options.verdict: The incentive is a planted detail and has no bearing on how missing values are treated.

options.text: It would make the median income of the completed sample differ from the original median.
options.verdict: Filling with the median leaves the median where it was, so this is not the concern.

options.text: It would reduce the sample size available for the comparison across the income bands.
options.verdict: Filling blanks keeps every respondent, so sample size is not what suffers.

options.text: It would move many older respondents into the middle band and distort the comparison.
options.verdict: Because the blanks cluster among older people, median filling changes who is in the middle band.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A grocery chain's supply team wants analytics to 'improve forecasting'. Forecast error for fresh produce is currently 28% at store-day level. The analyst asks what success looks like: the supply manager says 'better forecasts' and the finance manager says 'less waste'. The chain is also trialling self-checkout in five stores. What should the analyst do to define the future state?
why: Neither 'better forecasts' nor 'less waste' can be tested as stated. The future state needs measurable outcomes the stakeholders agree on, with forecast accuracy treated as a means to the waste outcome. A target chosen for technical or benchmarking reasons has no tie to this chain's objective.

options.text: Adopt 'better forecasts' as the objective, since forecasting is what the supply team asked for.
options.verdict: An objective with no measure cannot be used to judge whether the initiative succeeded.

options.text: Set the target at the lowest forecast error the data science team believes is technically achievable.
options.verdict: What is technically achievable is not the same as what the business needs or values.

options.text: Agree measurable outcomes with both managers, linking a waste target to the forecast error it needs.
options.verdict: This turns two vague aims into one testable outcome and makes forecast accuracy the means to it.

options.text: Benchmark forecast error against other grocery chains and adopt the industry median as the goal.
options.verdict: A benchmark gives context, but an industry median has no link to this chain's waste objective.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A pricing study for a ferry operator was meant to determine whether a 10% fare rise would reduce revenue. The analysis could estimate price sensitivity for tourists but not for commuters, because commuter fares have never changed. Commuters make up 65% of passengers. The board expects a clear recommendation on Friday. The operator's newest vessel enters service next week. What should the analyst recommend?
why: The results answer the question for a minority of passengers and are silent on the majority. An honest recommendation says so and proposes how to close the gap at limited risk. Borrowing tourist behaviour for commuters, doing nothing, or presenting a partial answer as complete each misstate what the evidence supports.

options.text: Raise all fares by 10%, applying the tourist price sensitivity to commuters as well.
options.verdict: Commuters and tourists are likely to respond differently, and nothing supports treating them alike.

options.text: Raise tourist fares only, and report that the commuter question has been answered.
options.verdict: Acting on the tourist result may be reasonable, but the commuter question remains open.

options.text: Leave all fares unchanged, since the analysis could not produce a complete answer.
options.verdict: An incomplete answer is a reason to gather evidence, not to stop.

options.text: Trial the fare change on some routes to learn how commuters respond, then decide.
options.verdict: A contained trial produces the missing evidence while limiting the revenue at risk.

trap: Treating a stakeholder's stated want as the research question
stem: A regional water utility's customer director asks the analytics lead for a real-time dashboard of call-centre volumes. The utility moved to a new billing platform in March, and the office kitchen is mid-renovation. When asked what prompted the request, the director says complaints to the ombudsman have doubled and the board wants to know why. The board paper is due in two weeks. What should the analyst do first?
why: The director named a deliverable, and the real problem only surfaced when the analyst asked: complaints have doubled and nobody knows why. Framing that problem decides whether a dashboard, a diagnostic study or something else is needed. The billing platform may become a hypothesis later; the kitchen is noise.

options.text: Clarify the business problem behind the request, the rise in complaints, before producing anything.
options.verdict: The doubling of complaints is the problem the board cares about, and it has to be framed before any deliverable can be judged useful.

options.text: Extract complaint and call records from the new billing platform and begin profiling them for quality.
options.verdict: Profiling is sound sourcing work, but which data matters depends on a problem that has not yet been framed.

options.text: Gather dashboard requirements from the call-centre team leaders so that the build can begin this week.
options.verdict: This takes the stated want as the need; a call-volume dashboard may say nothing about why ombudsman complaints doubled.

options.text: Propose a text-mining model over complaint narratives to classify the main drivers of escalation.
options.verdict: This selects a technique before the problem and the decision it supports have been defined.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Treating a governance or data management problem as a modelling choice
stem: At a health network, three analytics teams each maintain their own 'patient' table, and reports to the board disagree on patient counts. Each team's lead proposes a better matching algorithm to deduplicate their own table. The chief executive asks the analyst for a lasting fix. The network's intranet is being migrated. What should the analyst recommend?
why: The counts disagree because there are three versions of the same core entity with no shared definition or owner. Better matching inside each table produces three cleaner tables that still differ. A lasting fix is a governance one: a single mastered record, someone accountable for it and definitions everyone uses.

options.text: A rule that only the largest team's table may be used for reports going to the board.
options.verdict: Choosing a table by size does not make it correct or governed.

options.text: A reconciliation report produced before each board meeting to explain the differences.
options.verdict: Explaining the discrepancy each time manages the symptom indefinitely.

options.text: A governed master patient record, with a named owner and agreed definitions used by all teams.
options.verdict: One authoritative, owned record removes the source of the disagreement.

options.text: A more advanced matching algorithm, applied separately within each of the three team tables.
options.verdict: Each table would be tidier, and the three would still give different counts.

trap: Jumping to data or modelling before the research question is framed
stem: An energy retailer wants to use analytics to reduce bill-shock complaints. The analyst finds that customer service already produces a monthly complaints report in spreadsheets, that two teams define 'bill shock' differently, and that smart-meter data covers only 60% of customers. The sponsor is eager to see a predictive model and mentions that a rival retailer has one. What does the analyst most need to establish before defining what the initiative should achieve?
why: A future state can only be defined against a known starting point. Here the starting point includes two conflicting definitions, an existing report and partial data coverage, all of which constrain what is achievable. The rival's model and the sponsor's enthusiasm say nothing about where this organisation stands.

options.text: How the problem is measured and handled today, including the definitions and data in use.
options.verdict: Conflicting definitions and partial coverage are current-state facts that any target must be set against.

options.text: Whether smart meters can be rolled out to the remaining 40% of customers within the year.
options.verdict: Extending coverage is a possible later action, not the understanding needed to set objectives.

options.text: Which predictive algorithm the rival retailer uses, so the initiative can match its capability.
options.verdict: A competitor's tooling is not evidence of what this retailer's problem or starting point is.

options.text: What accuracy the sponsor would accept from a predictive model before it goes into production.
options.verdict: This assumes a predictive model is the answer before the current state has been understood.

trap: Treating a governance or data management problem as a modelling choice
stem: Two source systems at a telco each hold an 'active customer' flag. Billing counts anyone invoiced in the last 90 days; the CRM counts anyone with an open service. For a churn study, the analyst finds the flags disagree for 11% of customers. The data scientist says the model will 'learn around it'. The telco's financial year ends in June. What should the analyst do?
why: Churn can only be measured against an agreed meaning of 'active'. Two definitions disagreeing for 11% of customers is a definitional problem that belongs to the business owners, and no model can settle which one the study means. Dropping the disputed customers or picking a system on reputation both dodge the decision.

options.text: Use the billing flag, because financial systems are audited and are therefore more accurate.
options.verdict: Audited does not mean it is the right definition for this purpose, and the owners have not agreed.

options.text: Exclude the 11% of customers whose flags disagree, so that the remaining data is consistent.
options.verdict: The disputed customers are likely to include those near churn, so removing them biases the study.

options.text: Let the model use both flags as inputs, since more features generally improve accuracy.
options.verdict: A model cannot resolve which definition the study is measuring churn against.

options.text: Agree one definition of an active customer with the business owners and document it.
options.verdict: The study's outcome depends on what 'active' means, and that is a business decision to be recorded.

trap: Misreading what an output or measure actually shows
stem: A property management firm asks what a 'typical' tenant in arrears owes. The analyst explores the arrears balances and produces the summary below. The finance manager wants a single figure for the board paper. The firm recently opened a Brisbane office. Which figure best represents the typical tenant, and why?
why: The mean is more than four times the median and the largest balance is enormous, so the distribution is heavily skewed by a few accounts. Half of tenants owe $420 or less, which is what 'typical' asks for. The mean answers a different question: the total owed divided by the number of tenants.

options.text: The median of $420, because a few very large balances pull the mean upward.
options.verdict: Half of tenants owe this much or less, and the figure is unaffected by the handful of extreme balances.

options.text: The largest balance of $212,000, because it shows the board the scale of the exposure.
options.verdict: One extreme account describes the worst case, not the typical tenant.

options.text: The 90th percentile of $2,900, because it covers nearly all tenants in arrears.
options.verdict: This is a level nine in ten tenants are below, which marks the high end, not the centre.

options.text: The mean of $1,860, because it uses every tenant's balance in its calculation.
options.verdict: Using every value is why the mean is dragged far above what most tenants owe.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: The executive of a freight company has accepted a recommendation to adopt a route-optimisation model. The data scientist says the model is finished and can be 'switched on Monday'. Dispatchers have not seen it, the dispatch system needs an interface to receive routes, and nobody has been named to monitor the model's performance. The company's annual general meeting is next month. What should the analyst develop next?
why: An accepted recommendation and a finished model are not yet a working change. Three gaps stand between them and value: a system interface, dispatchers who have not seen the tool and no owner for its performance. An implementation plan closes those gaps. More tuning or more persuasion addresses none of them.

options.text: A second recommendation paper restating the business case for the model to the executive.
options.verdict: The executive has already agreed, so the case does not need to be made again.

options.text: A further round of model tuning, so that performance is maximised before the switch-on date.
options.verdict: The model is not what stands in the way of adoption.

options.text: A plan covering the system interface, dispatcher readiness, ownership and monitoring.
options.verdict: These are the gaps between a finished model and routes being used in dispatch.

options.text: A presentation for the annual general meeting announcing the adoption of route optimisation.
options.verdict: Announcing the change does nothing to make it work.

task: Assess the Analytics and System Approach Taken
trap: Misreading what an output or measure actually shows
stem: A utility's data scientist reports the results below for a model predicting water pipe failures, and proposes deploying it next month. The asset manager asks the analyst whether the approach is sound. The utility is also replacing its vehicle fleet. What does the comparison indicate?

exhibit.title: Pipe failure model: failures correctly identified

why: The model identifies failures far better in the data it learned from than in data it has not seen. The hold-out result is the guide to how it will perform in use, and a drop from 94% to 58% indicates it has fitted the particulars of the training data. Averaging the two or dismissing the test set hides that.

options.text: The test set is smaller than the training set, so its result can be set aside as unreliable.
options.verdict: Hold-out sets are normally smaller, and 8,000 pipes is ample to take the result seriously.

options.text: The model fits its training data far better than new data, so the approach needs revisiting.
options.verdict: The gap between the two results shows the model does not generalise to unseen pipes.

options.text: The model should be retrained on the 2024 data alone, as that is the most recent period.
options.verdict: Discarding five years of data does not address why the model fails on unseen records.

options.text: The model performs well overall, since the average across the two data sets is 76%.
options.verdict: Averaging mixes a flattering figure with the only one that predicts performance in use.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Choosing the most sophisticated technique when a simpler one answers it
stem: A mid-sized insurer's executive wants to 'become AI-first' and proposes buying an enterprise machine-learning platform. At present, monthly reports are compiled by hand from spreadsheets, the same metric differs between departments, and nobody owns data quality. A vendor demonstration is booked for next week. The insurer turned 50 this year. What should the analyst advise on analytics strategy?
why: The organisation cannot yet produce consistent basic reporting, so advanced tooling would sit on data nobody trusts or owns. Strategy at organisation level matches ambition to current capability and builds in sequence toward business priorities. Buying a platform or hiring specialists first assumes foundations that are not there.

options.text: Delay any investment until competitors' experience with similar platforms is published.
options.verdict: Waiting on others leaves known foundational problems unaddressed.

options.text: Buy the platform now, since advanced tools will drive improvement in the underlying data.
options.verdict: Tools do not fix inconsistent definitions or absent ownership; they inherit them.

options.text: Hire a team of data scientists first, so that the platform is used fully once it arrives.
options.verdict: Specialists would spend their time reconciling spreadsheets.

options.text: Build foundations first: consistent data, clear ownership and reliable basic reporting.
options.verdict: Advanced analytics depends on basics the insurer does not yet have.

trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: An insurer's claims team asks, 'Is our fraud process good?'. The analyst needs a research question that analytics can answer. The team investigates about 4% of claims, selected by assessor judgement, and confirms fraud in a quarter of those. The team's manager is retiring in June. Which reformulation is most useful?
why: The unanswered risk is in the 96% of claims nobody investigates. A question about those claims is specific, answerable with data and bears on whether selection should change. The hit rate among investigated claims is easy to compute but says nothing about what is being missed.

options.text: How satisfied are assessors with the current process for selecting claims to investigate?
options.verdict: Assessor satisfaction is measurable but does not indicate how well fraud is detected.

options.text: Among claims not selected for investigation, how many resemble the confirmed fraud cases?
options.verdict: This is specific and answerable, and it addresses the fraud the current process may be missing.

options.text: What share of investigated claims were confirmed as fraud in each of the past five years?
options.verdict: This is answerable, but it only describes the claims already selected and ignores the rest.

options.text: Is the fraud process good compared with the processes used by insurers of similar size?
options.verdict: This keeps the vague term 'good' and relies on comparison data the insurer is unlikely to hold.

trap: Skipping a stakeholder whose decision or data the work depends on
stem: For a study of emergency department waiting times, the analyst needs triage timestamps from the hospital's clinical system. An IT contractor offers a copy of last year's database backup from his laptop, which would save two weeks. The formal request to the data custodian takes ten working days. The executive has approved the research question. A new CT scanner is being installed. What should the analyst do?
why: Approval of the research question is not approval to obtain patient data by any route. The custodian controls access, and an informal copy on a laptop sits outside that control whatever is later done to it. The ten days can be spent on planning the analysis, so little is lost.

options.text: Request the data through the custodian and use the wait to prepare the analysis plan.
options.verdict: The custodian is the authorised route to patient data, and the wait can be used productively.

options.text: Accept the backup copy, but delete the patient identifiers before any analysis begins.
options.verdict: Removing identifiers afterwards does not make the way the data was obtained acceptable.

options.text: Accept the backup copy, since the executive has already approved the research question.
options.verdict: Approving the question does not authorise taking patient data from an uncontrolled copy.

options.text: Ask the executive to instruct the contractor in writing to release the backup copy.
options.verdict: This seeks to go around the custodian instead of using the access process that exists.

trap: Skipping a stakeholder whose decision or data the work depends on
stem: An analyst has completed an analysis of declining regional sales for a farm-machinery dealer and is about to prepare the report. The original sponsor, the sales director, left the company a month ago, and a new director started last week from a competitor. The analysis took three months, and the dealer's trade show is in ten days. Before preparing the communication, what should the analyst do?
why: The person who will act on the findings has changed since the questions were set. Before anything is written, the analyst needs to know what decision the new director faces and what they need from the work. A report built to the old brief, or a full technical dump, may miss the decision entirely.

options.text: Send the full technical analysis now, so that the new director can form an independent view.
options.verdict: Three months of unfiltered analysis leaves a newcomer to work out what matters.

options.text: Confirm with the new director what decision is pending and what they need from the findings.
options.verdict: The audience has changed, so its needs have to be re-established before the report is shaped.

options.text: Hold the findings until after the trade show, so that they receive the director's full attention.
options.verdict: Delay may withhold information the director needs for decisions being made now.

options.text: Prepare the report to the original brief, since the research questions were formally approved.
options.verdict: Approval by a departed sponsor does not mean the brief still fits the current decision-maker.

trap: Treating a stakeholder's stated want as the research question
stem: A council wants to use analytics to prioritise road resurfacing. Road segments are currently resurfaced on a fixed twelve-year cycle. The asset manager wants 'AI-driven predictive maintenance'; the chief financial officer wants the annual resurfacing budget held flat; residents report potholes through an app launched in May. The analyst is defining the desired future state. Which statement best serves the initiative?
why: A future state describes the outcome the organisation wants, within its constraints, in a form that can be measured. The correct statement does that and leaves the means open. Naming a platform describes a solution, shortening the cycle ignores the budget, and zero reports is neither realistic nor tied to condition.

options.text: Resident pothole reports through the app are reduced to zero within the first year of operation.
options.verdict: A zero target on one reporting channel is unrealistic and can be met by people not reporting.

options.text: An AI-driven predictive maintenance platform is implemented across the council's road asset register.
options.verdict: This describes a solution the asset manager wants, not the outcome the council is seeking.

options.text: Resurfacing is prioritised by measured condition and risk, within budget, with fewer defects.
options.verdict: This states a measurable outcome inside the budget constraint without prescribing how it is achieved.

options.text: The fixed cycle is shortened from twelve years to ten so that surfaces are renewed more often.
options.verdict: More frequent renewal breaks the flat-budget constraint and still ignores actual road condition.

trap: Treating correlation as causation
stem: Analysis for a gym chain shows that members who use the mobile app visit 40% more often than those who do not. The digital manager's draft slide reads 'The app increases visits by 40%'. Members choose for themselves whether to install the app. The chain is opening two new sites. How should the analyst word the insight?
why: Members opted in, so keener members may be both more likely to install the app and more likely to visit. The data shows a difference between the groups and cannot separate the app's effect from that self-selection. The honest insight states the association and its limit, without claiming the reverse or denying any link.

options.text: App users visit more often, but the data cannot show that the app is the cause.
options.verdict: This reports what was observed and is clear that self-selection prevents a causal reading.

options.text: The app increases visits by 40%, so promoting installation will lift attendance.
options.verdict: Members chose to install it, so the difference may reflect who installs, not what the app does.

options.text: Frequent visitors cause app installations, so the app has no effect on attendance.
options.verdict: The reverse direction is equally unproven, and it does not rule out an app effect.

options.text: The app has no relationship with visits, because members self-select into using it.
options.verdict: Self-selection limits causal claims; it does not erase the observed association.

trap: Doing data science or data engineering work instead of the analysis role
stem: A mid-sized manufacturer is starting its first analytics initiative, on machine downtime. The team is a business analyst, a data engineer and a contracted data scientist. During planning, the data scientist asks the analyst to select and tune the modelling algorithm, saying 'you know the business'. The plant manager wants to approve the initiative's plan by Friday, and the canteen contract is up for renewal. Where should the analyst focus?
why: In an analytics team the analyst's contribution is the business framing: what is being asked, how success is judged and how results will be used. Algorithm selection and tuning belong to the data scientist, pipelines to the engineer, and a resource schedule is project management. Knowing the business is the reason to stay on the framing.

options.text: On building the data pipeline with the engineer so that modelling can start as early as possible.
options.verdict: Pipeline construction is data engineering and does not define what the initiative is for.

options.text: On a detailed schedule and resource plan so that the plant manager can approve the work by Friday.
options.verdict: Scheduling and resourcing are project management and leave the analytics approach undefined.

options.text: On selecting and tuning the algorithm, since business knowledge determines which model performs best.
options.verdict: Model selection and tuning are the data scientist's work, whatever the analyst knows of the business.

options.text: On the research questions, the success measures and how the plant will use the results.
options.verdict: These are the elements only the analyst is placed to supply, and the plan cannot be approved without them.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Treating a governance or data management problem as a modelling choice
stem: A retailer's analytics teams clean the same address errors in customer data before each project. The errors arise at store checkouts, where staff type addresses free-form. The head of analytics proposes a shared cleansing script. Store managers say checkout speed is their priority. The retailer's Christmas catalogue is in production. What should the data strategy address?
why: The errors are created at capture and corrected downstream, again and again. A strategy-level response fixes quality where the data is created and makes someone there accountable for it. A shared script makes the rework more efficient without ending it, and a model or an exclusion rule works around the cause.

options.text: A machine-learning model that predicts the correct address from the mistyped entry.
options.verdict: A model is an elaborate way of repairing data that could be captured correctly.

options.text: Fixing capture at the checkout, with accountability for quality where the data is created.
options.verdict: Correcting the source stops the errors instead of repairing them on every project.

options.text: A shared cleansing script, so that every analytics project applies the same corrections.
options.verdict: This standardises the rework but leaves new errors arriving every day.

options.text: A policy that analytics projects exclude customers whose addresses contain errors.
options.verdict: Excluding affected customers shrinks and biases every analysis.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A bank's analyst is planning data collection for a study of why small-business customers close their accounts. The fastest source is call recordings, which contain customers' personal details. The privacy office has not been consulted, and the compliance calendar shows an audit next quarter. A colleague suggests transcribing all the recordings with a cloud speech service this week. What should the collection plan include before any data is gathered?
why: Call recordings hold personal information, and sending them to an external service is a use that has to be permitted before it happens. Confirming permitted use, privacy and security requirements is part of planning collection. Speed, sample design and the audit date are secondary to whether the data may be used this way.

options.text: Confirmation from the privacy office that the recordings may be used in this way.
options.verdict: Personal data cannot be sent to an outside service until its permitted use has been established.

options.text: A sampling scheme selecting the longest recordings, as they contain the most information.
options.verdict: Choosing long calls would bias the sample, and sampling still presumes the data may be used.

options.text: A schedule that finishes the collection before the compliance audit begins next quarter.
options.verdict: Finishing ahead of an audit does not make an unapproved use of personal data acceptable.

options.text: A contract with the cloud speech service so that transcription can begin without delay.
options.verdict: This arranges the processing before anyone has confirmed that the processing is allowed.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Being led by an irrelevant detail planted in the scenario
stem: A supermarket chain tested loyalty-app push notifications in 20 stores against 20 matched stores for eight weeks. Basket size and visit frequency did not differ between the groups, and the plausible range for any effect was narrow and centred on zero. The digital team has spent $200,000 building the feature and asks the analyst to recommend a national rollout 'to give it time to work'. Easter trading starts soon. What should the analyst recommend?
why: A well-matched test with a narrow range around zero is good evidence that the feature does nothing measurable. The $200,000 is already spent whichever way the decision goes, so it is not a reason to spend more. Recommending against rollout is a legitimate outcome of analysis.

options.text: Repeat the same test for another eight weeks in the same stores before deciding.
options.verdict: The result was precise, not inconclusive, so repeating it is unlikely to change the answer.

options.text: Roll out nationally and reassess in a year, when more data will be available.
options.verdict: The test already answered the question, and a national rollout is an expensive way to ask again.

options.text: Roll out nationally, since the amount already spent would otherwise be wasted.
options.verdict: Money already spent cannot be recovered by spending more on something that does not work.

options.text: Do not roll out in the current form, since the test shows no effect worth the cost.
options.verdict: The test was sound and found nothing, so further spending has no evidence behind it.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: An analyst is preparing customer data for a churn model. After the customer table is joined to the support-ticket table, the row count rises from 50,000 to 68,000. The data scientist says more rows will help training. The marketing team is waiting on the results for a campaign. What should the analyst check?
why: There are 50,000 customers, so 68,000 rows after a join means some customers now appear more than once, most likely one row per ticket. Those customers would be over-weighted in training. Extra rows from duplication are not extra information, and the fix is to aggregate tickets to one row per customer.

options.text: Whether the additional rows improve the model's accuracy when it is trained on them.
options.verdict: Accuracy measured on duplicated data would be misleading and would not expose the fault.

options.text: Whether the marketing campaign can be delayed until a larger sample is collected.
options.verdict: Sample size is not the issue, and the campaign timing is a distraction.

options.text: Whether the join has duplicated customers who have more than one support ticket.
options.verdict: The extra 18,000 rows can only be repeats of existing customers, which would distort the model.

options.text: Whether the support-ticket table should be dropped to return the count to 50,000.
options.verdict: Ticket history is likely to be informative; the join needs correcting, not abandoning.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A bank has rolled out self-service dashboards to 300 managers. Usage logs show that 80% have never opened one. In interviews, managers say they do not know how to read the charts or what action a number implies. The head of analytics proposes adding 40 more dashboards. The bank's graduate intake starts in February. What should the talent strategy prioritise?
why: The managers have said why they do not use the dashboards: they cannot interpret them or connect them to action. That is a skills gap among the consumers of analytics, and a talent strategy covers them as well as the specialists. More dashboards, prettier dashboards or fewer users each sidestep it.

options.text: Hiring visualisation specialists, so that the existing dashboards look more appealing.
options.verdict: Appearance is not what the managers said was stopping them.

options.text: Building managers' data literacy, so that they can interpret and act on the figures.
options.verdict: The stated barrier is skill in reading and using data, which the strategy can address directly.

options.text: Restricting dashboards to analysts, since managers have shown they will not use them.
options.verdict: This gives up on data-informed management instead of enabling it.

options.text: Adding the 40 dashboards, so that every manager finds one relevant to their role.
options.verdict: More of something managers cannot read will not raise use.

trap: Jumping to data or modelling before the research question is framed
stem: A national parcel carrier has acquired three years of driver telematics data and a licence for a machine-learning platform. The chief operating officer wants the analytics team to 'find something valuable in it' before the licence renewal in six months. A data engineer has loaded the data and offers to run clustering over it tonight. The business analyst assigned to the initiative has not yet met the operations managers. What is the best next step?
why: The data and the tool exist, but no business problem does. Analytics work starts from a problem or opportunity the business owns, and the operations managers are the unconsulted source of one. The licence renewal date creates urgency without changing where the work has to begin.

options.text: Assess the telematics data for completeness and accuracy so that later analysis rests on sound inputs.
options.verdict: Data assessment is legitimate, but it is premature while nobody knows which questions the data must answer.

options.text: Draft a benefits case for the platform licence so the renewal decision is supported in six months.
options.verdict: This responds to the licence deadline rather than to the absence of a business problem.

options.text: Meet the operations managers to identify the problems or opportunities the data might address.
options.verdict: The initiative has data and tooling but no business problem, and the people who hold the problems have not been asked.

options.text: Let the clustering run proceed and review the resulting groups for patterns that suggest a use case.
options.verdict: Exploration without a question produces patterns that no one has a decision waiting for.

trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: The chief financial officer of a retail group has ten minutes at the next executive meeting to decide whether to close six under-performing stores. The analyst's work includes a store-profitability model, sensitivity analysis and customer-overlap maps. The data scientist wants to present the model's validation statistics first. The group's annual report is at the printer. What does the CFO most need?
why: The audience is a decision-maker with ten minutes and one decision. What serves that need is the recommendation, what it is worth and what could go wrong, with supporting detail held ready. Validation statistics, maps and sensitivity runs are evidence behind the answer, not the answer.

options.text: The model's validation statistics, so that the CFO can judge whether to trust the results.
options.verdict: Trust matters, but leading with validation spends the ten minutes on method.

options.text: A walkthrough of the sensitivity analysis, covering each assumption that was varied.
options.verdict: The single most important sensitivity belongs in the risk; the full walkthrough does not fit.

options.text: All customer-overlap maps for the six stores, so the CFO can inspect the evidence directly.
options.verdict: Raw evidence asks the CFO to do the analysis in the meeting.

options.text: The recommendation, its financial effect and the main risk, with detail available on request.
options.verdict: This is what a decision in ten minutes requires, and the supporting evidence stays on hand.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A fast-food franchisor asks whether extending opening hours to midnight lifts profit. Head office holds daily sales totals for all 140 stores; 30 stores also keep hourly sales and hourly labour cost, and twelve of those 30 already open until midnight. The marketing team is planning a new burger launch. Which data set best supports the research question?
why: Profit from late opening is revenue earned in the extra hours less the cost of staffing them. Only the hourly data isolates those hours and includes labour cost. Daily totals cover more stores but cannot separate late trade, and stated intentions in a survey are not profit.

options.text: Daily sales totals for the twelve late-opening stores, before and after their hours changed.
options.verdict: A before-and-after view of sales omits labour cost, so it cannot answer a profit question.

options.text: Customer survey responses on whether people would visit if stores opened until midnight.
options.verdict: Stated intention is weak evidence of behaviour and carries no information about profit.

options.text: Hourly sales and labour cost from the 30 stores, comparing late openers with the rest.
options.verdict: This is the only data that isolates the extra hours and includes the cost of staffing them.

options.text: Daily sales totals for all 140 stores, because more stores give more reliable results.
options.verdict: More stores do not help when daily totals cannot separate late-night trade or its cost.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: A university introduces an early-warning indicator that flags students at risk of failing. Academic staff object that it 'reduces students to numbers', and some refuse to use it. The analytics team's only response so far is an email explaining the model's accuracy. Student advisers, who would act on the flags, have not been consulted about workflow. Exams begin in three weeks. What should the analyst do?
why: The objection is about what the indicator means for professional judgement, and an accuracy email does not speak to it. The advisers who must act were never asked how it fits their work. Engaging both groups on how the flag is used addresses the concern; mandating or withdrawing it avoids the conversation.

options.text: Engage academics and advisers on how the flag supports their judgement, and adjust the process.
options.verdict: The resistance is about role and workflow, which is resolved by involving the people affected.

options.text: Withdraw the indicator until every academic has agreed in writing to use it.
options.verdict: Unanimity is an unrealistic bar that would deny students the support meanwhile.

options.text: Send a second email with more detailed accuracy statistics and a description of the algorithm.
options.verdict: More technical evidence answers a question the academics did not ask.

options.text: Ask the vice-chancellor to mandate use of the indicator by all academic staff.
options.verdict: Compulsion may secure compliance on paper while leaving the objection in place.

trap: Wrong analytics type for the question
stem: A logistics firm's on-time delivery rate fell from 96% to 89% over the past quarter. Operations managers want to stop the decline, and the analyst is drafting research questions. The firm also opened a new depot in Townsville during the quarter. Which question should come first in the sequence?
why: Before asking why performance fell, or what will happen next, the firm needs to know where and when it fell. That descriptive picture narrows the diagnostic work and tests whether the Townsville depot is even implicated. Predictive and prescriptive questions depend on understanding that does not exist yet.

options.text: What routing changes would maximise on-time delivery at the lowest cost?
options.verdict: Optimising routes presumes routing is the cause before the decline has been located.

options.text: Where and when did on-time performance fall, by depot, route and week?
options.verdict: Locating the decline comes first, because it tells the firm where to look for causes.

options.text: Which deliveries in the coming quarter are most likely to arrive late?
options.verdict: Prediction comes after the firm understands what has happened and why.

options.text: Did the opening of the Townsville depot cause the fall in on-time delivery?
options.verdict: This commits to one suspected cause before the data shows where the decline sits.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A predictive model at a rail operator identifies, with good accuracy, which track sections are likely to develop faults within 90 days. The maintenance planning team currently schedules inspections on a fixed calendar. The analyst is asked what to recommend. The operator's timetable changes in December. Which recommendation turns the result into value?
why: A prediction has no value until a decision changes because of it. Here the decision is where to inspect, so the recommendation is to schedule by predicted risk and to measure whether faults fall. Publishing predictions, polishing accuracy or widening scope leave the calendar-based practice untouched.

options.text: Publish the model's fault predictions on the intranet for all maintenance staff to consult.
options.verdict: Making predictions available does not change how inspections are scheduled.

options.text: Extend the model to predict faults in signalling equipment and rolling stock as well.
options.verdict: Broader scope adds more predictions while the first set remains unused.

options.text: Improve the model's accuracy further before proposing any change to current practice.
options.verdict: The model is already accurate enough to use, and waiting delays the benefit.

options.text: Prioritise inspections on the sections the model flags, and measure the effect on faults.
options.verdict: This changes the decision the prediction was built to inform and checks that it works.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: An analyst at a logistics company is collecting scanner data from depots for a study of parcel mis-sorts. The collection plan specifies six months of scans from all 14 depots. Four depots send files with timestamps in local time rather than UTC, and one depot's file is missing March. The project manager wants analysis to start tomorrow. The company's fleet is being rebranded. What should the analyst do?
why: The collected data does not yet match the plan: timestamps are inconsistent and a month is absent. Recording the discrepancies, obtaining the real data and reconciling formats is part of collection. Starting with a subset or inventing March would build the analysis on data that differs from what was specified.

options.text: Hand all the files to the data scientist, since robust models tolerate such inconsistencies.
options.verdict: A model cannot detect that timestamps are in different time zones or that a month is absent.

options.text: Record the discrepancies, obtain the missing month and reconcile the time formats before use.
options.verdict: Collection is complete only when the data matches the plan, and these gaps are known and fixable.

options.text: Start the analysis with the ten consistent depots and add the other four when time allows.
options.verdict: Dropping four depots changes the scope of the study and may hide where mis-sorts occur.

options.text: Convert the files and fill March for the affected depot with the average of adjacent months.
options.verdict: Invented figures for a missing month would be analysed as though they were observations.

trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A study for a regional bank asked why mortgage applications from first-home buyers fell. The analysis shows that applications fell 22%, that the fall is concentrated in three postcodes, and that in those postcodes a competitor opened branches offering a fee waiver. The analyst is drafting the key insight. The bank's chief executive is speaking at a conference next week. Which statement is the insight?
why: The research question was why applications fell. An insight connects the findings into an answer to that question: the fall sits where the competitor's offer appeared. The 22% restates the problem, the method statement describes the work, and the claim about buyer confidence goes beyond anything the analysis found.

options.text: First-home buyer mortgage applications fell by 22% over the period that was analysed.
options.verdict: This is a finding that restates the problem and does not explain it.

options.text: The analysis used application records from all branches and was validated against finance data.
options.verdict: This describes method, which supports credibility but is not an insight.

options.text: The fall sits where a competitor launched a fee waiver, suggesting local price competition.
options.verdict: This links the findings into an explanation that answers the question the study was asked.

options.text: First-home buyers across the region are losing confidence in the housing market.
options.verdict: Nothing in the analysis measured confidence, and the fall was confined to three postcodes.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A council begins using a model to target building-compliance inspections. After three months, inspectors report that the model keeps sending them to the same low-income suburbs, where past inspections were concentrated, and residents have complained. Detection rates per inspection are up. The compliance manager wants to continue as is. The council's new bin collection schedule starts on Monday. What should the analyst raise?
why: The model learned from where inspectors went before, so it finds breaches where it has always looked and sends inspectors back there. A rising detection rate is consistent with that loop and does not show the targeting is fair or complete. The effect on residents is a consequence of the change that needs review.

options.text: The model may be reinforcing past inspection patterns, so its inputs and effects need review.
options.verdict: Training on where inspections happened before can lock the council into inspecting the same places.

options.text: The detection rate is up, so the complaints should be handled by the communications team.
options.verdict: A higher rate in the suburbs already targeted does not show the targeting is sound.

options.text: The model needs more data from the same suburbs, so that its predictions become more precise.
options.verdict: More data from the same places would strengthen the loop that is causing the problem.

options.text: The inspectors need further training, so that they follow the model's targeting consistently.
options.verdict: The inspectors are raising a valid concern, not failing to comply.

trap: Misreading what an output or measure actually shows
stem: A café chain models weekly store revenue. The output below is from a linear regression on 180 store-weeks. The regional manager asks what the model says about local advertising. The chain's head barista has just won a national award. Which reading of the advertising result is correct?
why: The advertising coefficient has a p-value of 0.62, so an estimate of this size could easily arise if advertising had no relationship with revenue. The $45 cannot be relied on. A p-value is not a share of variation explained, and a high p-value does not indicate a negative effect.

options.text: Each $100 of local advertising reliably adds $45 of weekly revenue, so spend should rise.
options.verdict: This reads the coefficient while ignoring that its p-value gives no grounds for relying on it.

options.text: Local advertising explains 62% of the variation in weekly revenue across the stores.
options.verdict: This confuses the p-value with R-squared, which is 0.58 and describes the whole model.

options.text: Local advertising reduces weekly revenue, because its p-value is higher than the others.
options.verdict: A p-value says nothing about direction; the coefficient is positive and simply uncertain.

options.text: The data does not show a reliable relationship between local advertising and weekly revenue.
options.verdict: With a p-value of 0.62 the estimate is indistinguishable from no relationship.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A model built for a recruitment firm ranks candidates for interview. Analysis shows it performs well overall, but it ranks candidates with career gaps lower, and career gaps are far more common among women in the data. The client is delighted with the time saved and wants the model rolled out to all roles next month. The firm has just moved offices. What should the analyst recommend?
why: The model is disadvantaging a group through a characteristic that stands in for gender, which is an ethical and legal exposure regardless of overall accuracy. A recommendation has to account for that before use is widened. Removing the gender field leaves the proxy in place, and abandoning the model forgoes a fix that may be possible.

options.text: Proceed with the rollout, but remove the gender field from the data used by the model.
options.verdict: Career gaps would still act as a stand-in for gender, so the effect would remain.

options.text: Withdraw the model permanently, since any model trained on past hiring will be biased.
options.verdict: This discards the benefit without first establishing whether the disparity can be corrected.

options.text: Pause the wider rollout until the disparity is investigated and addressed with the client.
options.verdict: The disparity is a known harm, and extending the model would extend it.

options.text: Proceed with the rollout, since the model's overall performance meets the agreed target.
options.verdict: Overall performance does not offset a systematic disadvantage to one group.

trap: Technique mismatched to the data or the outcome type
stem: A lender wants to estimate the probability that a loan applicant will default, using income, existing debts and length of employment. The outcome in the historical data is recorded as defaulted or not defaulted. The analyst is drafting the analysis plan with the data scientist. The lender's branch network is being reduced. Which technique should the plan specify?
why: The outcome has two categories and the lender wants a probability. Logistic regression is built for that. Linear regression assumes a continuous outcome and can return values below zero or above one, clustering has no outcome to predict, and the years over which loans were written do not make this a forecasting problem.

options.text: Time series forecasting, because the loans in the historical data were written over several years.
options.verdict: The task is to predict an outcome per applicant, not to project a quantity through time.

options.text: Logistic regression, because the outcome being predicted has only two possible categories.
options.verdict: It models the probability of a two-category outcome, which is what the lender has asked for.

options.text: Linear regression, because the predictors are numeric and the relationship can be quantified.
options.verdict: The choice turns on the outcome, not the predictors, and a yes/no outcome does not suit a straight-line model.

options.text: Cluster analysis, because applicants can be grouped into segments with similar risk profiles.
options.verdict: Clustering finds groups without reference to an outcome, so it does not estimate default probability.

trap: Right action, wrong stage
stem: A retailer has agreed its research question: do customers who use click-and-collect spend more in store when they pick up? The analyst is planning data collection. A developer offers to start pulling every table from the e-commerce database 'in case it's useful'. The loyalty team mentions that a third of in-store purchases are made without a loyalty card. Head office is relocating. What should the plan address first?
why: The question depends on connecting a pickup to an in-store purchase by the same customer. With a third of purchases made without a card, that link is the main risk to answering the question at all, so the plan starts there. Bulk extraction, cleansing and reporting all assume the link exists.

options.text: A dashboard design for reporting click-and-collect spending once the data has been gathered.
options.verdict: Reporting design belongs to a later stage and assumes the data can answer the question.

options.text: A full extract of the e-commerce database, so that no potentially useful table is left out.
options.verdict: Collecting everything defers the thinking and does not show whether the needed link exists.

options.text: Which data the question needs, and whether pickups can be linked to in-store purchases.
options.verdict: The question cannot be answered unless pickups and purchases can be tied together, so that is planned first.

options.text: A cleansing routine for the loyalty data, so that duplicate member records are removed.
options.verdict: Cleansing is preparation work that follows once the required data has been identified.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: An insurer plans to replace claims assessors' manual triage with an analytics-driven priority score. The model is ready and the claims system can display the score. Assessors have had no involvement, and team leaders' bonuses are tied to the existing triage targets. The programme sponsor asks whether the organisation is ready. The insurer has a new advertising campaign on television. What is the analyst's best assessment?
why: Readiness covers people and incentives as well as technology. The system can show the score, but those who must use it have not been involved and their leaders are rewarded for the old way of working. Those conditions predict resistance, and a user guide does not change an incentive.

options.text: Ready, provided the assessors are sent a user guide in the week before go-live.
options.verdict: Instructions do not create involvement or realign bonuses tied to the old targets.

options.text: Not ready, since the model should be validated again on more recent claims first.
options.verdict: Nothing in the scenario questions the model; the gaps are organisational.

options.text: Ready, since the model is complete and the claims system can display the score.
options.verdict: This judges readiness on technology alone and ignores those who must use it.

options.text: Technically ready, but the people and incentives are not, which needs addressing.
options.verdict: The technology works, while involvement and reward structures still pull against the change.

trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: A year-long analytics programme at a port authority produces monthly findings on vessel turnaround. Terminal operators, who must act on the findings, say they learned of the first two months' results only through a newsletter. The harbour master receives a detailed dashboard he does not open. The programme director asks the analyst to fix communication. A new crane arrives in August. What should the analyst do first?
why: Both symptoms point to a plan built without asking the audiences what they need: the people who must act are under-served and the harbour master gets a format he does not use. The fix starts with finding out what each group needs, how often and in what form. Tweaking existing channels repeats the guess.

options.text: Add the terminal operators to the distribution list for the harbour master's dashboard.
options.verdict: This extends a format that is already going unused to a second audience.

options.text: Ask each stakeholder group what they need, how often and in what form, then revise the plan.
options.verdict: The current plan misfires for both groups, so their actual needs have to be established first.

options.text: Increase the newsletter to fortnightly, so that findings reach the operators more quickly.
options.verdict: More frequent delivery through a channel that failed them does not meet their need.

options.text: Run dashboard training for the harbour master, so that the existing reporting is used.
options.verdict: This assumes the dashboard is right and the reader is the problem, which nobody has checked.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A state library service will use a demand model to reallocate book stock among its 60 branches. The model was validated on historical loans. Branch managers are sceptical, and moving stock is costly to reverse. The service's director wants all 60 branches changed in a single weekend to 'get it done'. The library's logo was refreshed last year. What should the implementation plan propose?
why: The change is costly to reverse, has been tested only against history and faces sceptical managers. A pilot with agreed measures limits the exposure, produces live evidence and gives sceptics something to judge. A single weekend stakes everything on back-testing; another year of validation adds no live evidence at all.

options.text: A further year of historical validation before any stock is moved between branches.
options.verdict: More back-testing delays the change without showing how it performs in real branches.

options.text: A single-weekend changeover for all 60 branches, as the director has requested.
options.verdict: A change that is costly to undo should not rest entirely on historical validation.

options.text: A pilot in a few branches against agreed success measures, followed by staged rollout.
options.verdict: This tests the model in practice where the cost of being wrong is contained.

options.text: A rollout to branches whose managers volunteer, leaving the sceptical ones unchanged.
options.verdict: Volunteers are not a fair test, and this leaves the scepticism unaddressed.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A hospital network wants to reduce operating theatre cancellations. The analyst interviews the surgical director, who wants to know which surgeons run over time. Theatre nurses say cancellations follow late bed availability; the bed manager says discharge paperwork is the bottleneck. The finance partner wants only a dollar figure. Car park fees rose last month. How should the analyst treat these differing views?
why: Each stakeholder holds a different explanation and a different decision. At this stage those are hypotheses and needs to be captured, not competing answers to be settled by rank or by vote. Together they define the candidate research questions the analysis can then test.

options.text: Record each as a perspective on the problem and use them to shape candidate research questions.
options.verdict: The differing explanations are hypotheses, and capturing all of them is what gives the analysis something to test.

options.text: Adopt the surgical director's view, as the most senior clinical stakeholder sets the direction.
options.verdict: Seniority does not make one explanation of the cancellations more likely to be correct.

options.text: Run a survey of all theatre staff to establish which explanation has majority support.
options.verdict: A vote measures opinion about the cause, which is not the same as evidence of it.

options.text: Start with the finance partner's dollar figure, since a quantified loss will focus the others.
options.verdict: Sizing the loss is useful, but it sets aside the explanations that determine what to analyse.

task: Assess the Analytics and System Approach Taken
trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: An analytics team at a hardware chain was asked which product bundles to offer in order to raise average basket value. After six weeks the team presents a well-validated model predicting which customers will shop in the next 30 days. The model is accurate and the team is proud of it. The merchandising manager looks puzzled. The chain sponsors a local football club. As the analyst reviewing the work, what is the appropriate assessment?
why: The question was which bundles to offer; the model predicts who will shop. However accurate, it answers a different question, and assessing the approach means testing results against the research question, not against technical quality. Adding features or educating the manager would not make it address bundling.

options.text: The model is accurate and validated, so it should be delivered as the initiative's result.
options.verdict: Technical quality does not make an answer to the wrong question useful.

options.text: The work does not address the bundling question, so the approach should be redirected to it.
options.verdict: Results are judged against the research question, and this model answers another one.

options.text: The merchandising manager should be trained in predictive models before the handover.
options.verdict: The manager's puzzlement is warranted, and training would not make the work relevant.

options.text: The model should be extended with more features until it can also suggest bundles.
options.verdict: A model of who will shop is the wrong starting point for a question about product combinations.

task: Document and Communicate Findings from Completed Analysis
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: An analyst is finalising a report on why a telco's fibre installations run late. The analysis found that 70% of delays trace to incomplete address data at order entry. The draft describes the methodology across twelve pages and ends with the finding. The operations director, who commissioned the work, must decide what to change. A new CRM release is due in spring. What is missing from the report?
why: The director commissioned the work to decide what to change, and the draft stops at what was found. Documented findings need to carry through to what they mean for the decision, how far they can be relied on and what could be done. More method, more records or an industry comparison add volume without that.

options.text: A comparison with the late-installation rates published by other telcos in the market.
options.verdict: Benchmarks add context but do not turn the finding into something to act on.

options.text: A longer methodology section, so that each analytical step can be reproduced in full.
options.verdict: Twelve pages of method is already more than the director needs.

options.text: What the finding means for the director's decision, with limitations and options.
options.verdict: The report exists to support a decision, and it currently ends before reaching it.

options.text: An appendix listing every delayed installation, so that the director can verify the 70%.
options.verdict: Record-level listings do not help the director decide what to change.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: Analysis for a food-delivery platform shows that customers whose order arrives more than ten minutes late are three times as likely never to order again. Late deliveries cluster between 6 and 8 pm in four suburbs. The analyst presents this to the operations lead, who says 'interesting' and moves to the next agenda item. The platform's logo is being refreshed. What should the analyst have brought?
why: The analysis identified where and when the damage occurs, which is enough to propose what to do about it. Presented as a finding alone, it gave the operations lead nothing to decide. Deeper breakdowns, stronger tests or wider scope all extend the analysis instead of converting it into action.

options.text: Recommended actions for the peak-period suburbs, with the expected effect and cost of each.
options.verdict: A finding becomes useful when it arrives with options the decision-maker can choose between.

options.text: A stronger statistical test to confirm that late delivery is linked to customer loss.
options.verdict: The link was not in dispute; what was missing was a proposal.

options.text: A request for budget to extend the analysis to the platform's other capital cities.
options.verdict: Widening the study postpones acting on what is already known.

options.text: A more detailed breakdown of late deliveries by courier, restaurant and day of the week.
options.verdict: More detail deepens the description without telling the operations lead what to do.

trap: Choosing the most sophisticated technique when a simpler one answers it
stem: A streaming service showed a new sign-up page to half of its new visitors, chosen at random; the other half saw the old page.
