After two weeks, 4.1% of 50,000 visitors converted on the new page and 3.8% of 50,000 on the old. The product manager asks whether the difference is real. A data scientist offers to build a gradient-boosted model of conversion. The service also added three documentaries that fortnight. What analysis answers the question?
why: Visitors were assigned at random, so the two groups differ only in the page they saw, and anything else that fortnight affected both alike. Whether the gap is larger than chance would produce is answered by a test comparing the two rates. A predictive model, a forecast or a segmentation each answer other questions.

options.text: A time series forecast of conversions, to see whether the fortnight was above trend.
options.verdict: Both groups shared the same fortnight, so a trend comparison cannot separate the pages.

options.text: A gradient-boosted model predicting conversion from visitor and page characteristics.
options.verdict: A predictive model is far more than the question needs and does not test the difference directly.

options.text: A cluster analysis of converting visitors, to find the segments the new page attracts.
options.verdict: Segmenting converters describes who converted, not whether the new page performed better.

options.text: A test of the difference between the two conversion rates from the randomised groups.
options.verdict: Random assignment makes a direct comparison of the two rates the complete answer.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Treating a governance or data management problem as a modelling choice
stem: Analysts at a university estimate that a third of their time goes on working out what fields mean and where data came from. The same field name means different things in the student and finance systems. The chief information officer proposes buying faster analytics servers. A new enterprise agreement is being negotiated. Which investment addresses the problem?
why: The time is lost to not knowing what data means or where it originates, which is a metadata problem. A glossary and catalogue recording definitions, sources and owners removes that search. Faster servers speed up queries, not understanding, and copying everything into one place moves the ambiguity without resolving it.

options.text: A data lake that copies every system's tables into one location in their original form.
options.verdict: Co-locating the tables leaves the conflicting field meanings exactly as they are.

options.text: A business glossary and metadata catalogue recording definitions, sources and owners.
options.verdict: This supplies the missing knowledge about what each field means and where it comes from.

options.text: Faster analytics servers, so that queries return results in less time than they do now.
options.verdict: Query speed is not where the analysts' time is going.

options.text: Additional analysts, so that the time lost to data questions is offset by more staff.
options.verdict: More people would each lose the same third of their time.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: Midway through reporting on a study of patient no-shows at a clinic network, the analyst learns that clinic managers assumed the study covered all 18 clinics, whereas the data came only from the nine using the new booking system. The draft says 'no-show rates fell 12% after SMS reminders'. The chief executive wants a one-page summary by Thursday. The clinics' car parks are being resealed. What should the analyst do before reporting?
why: Stakeholders hold a wrong belief about what the study covered, and the headline would be read as a network-wide result. Correcting that understanding and stating the scope lets the finding be used for what it is. Generalising, withholding or stripping the number each handle the mismatch badly.

options.text: Check stakeholders' understanding of scope and state which clinics the result covers.
options.verdict: The finding is sound for nine clinics, and readers need to know that is what it describes.

options.text: Remove the 12% figure from the summary and describe the result in qualitative terms only.
options.verdict: Dropping the number loses the finding without fixing the misunderstanding about scope.

options.text: Withhold the findings until the remaining nine clinics can be added to the analysis.
options.verdict: The result is useful now if its scope is made clear, and the summary is due Thursday.

options.text: Report the 12% reduction as a network-wide result, since nine clinics are a large sample.
options.verdict: The nine were not chosen at random; they share a booking system the others lack.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A hospital is building a model to predict, at admission, which patients will be readmitted within 30 days. Preparing the data, the analyst notices a field 'discharge follow-up call made', populated after discharge and strongly associated with readmission. The data scientist is pleased: including it lifts accuracy from 71% to 93%. The hospital is celebrating its centenary. What should the analyst advise?
why: The model is meant to work at admission, and this field does not exist until after discharge. Its predictive strength comes from information the model would never have when used, so the 93% is an illusion. Down-weighting keeps the fault, and stripping every correlated field removes legitimate predictors.

options.text: Include the field, but reduce its weight so that the model does not rely on it alone.
options.verdict: A smaller weight still feeds the model information it will not have at admission.

options.text: Exclude the field, because it would not be known at the time the prediction is made.
options.verdict: Information recorded after discharge cannot be an input to a prediction made at admission.

options.text: Exclude all fields correlated with readmission, to prevent the model from overfitting.
options.verdict: Correlation with the outcome is what makes a legitimate predictor useful; timing is the fault here.

options.text: Include the field, because it is the strongest predictor of readmission in the data.
options.verdict: Its strength comes from being recorded after the event, so the accuracy gain will vanish in use.

trap: Choosing the most sophisticated technique when a simpler one answers it
stem: A regional airline wants to know which of its 22 routes lost money last financial year, and by how much, to inform a network review in three weeks. Finance holds revenue and cost by flight. A data scientist proposes building a neural-network profitability forecast. The airline's loyalty programme was relaunched in January. Which approach should the analyst plan?
why: The question is about what happened last year, the data to answer it exists, and the deadline is three weeks. That is a descriptive question with a descriptive answer. Forecasting, optimisation and a loyalty study each answer a different question from the one the network review has asked.

options.text: A prescriptive optimisation model recommending the network that maximises total profit.
options.verdict: Optimisation may follow the review, but it is not what was asked and will not fit the time.

options.text: A diagnostic study of how the loyalty relaunch changed demand on each of the routes.
options.verdict: The loyalty relaunch is a planted detail and not the subject of the question.

options.text: A neural-network forecast of route profitability trained on the flight-level finance data.
options.verdict: A forecast addresses future profitability, which the review has not asked about.

options.text: A descriptive analysis of profitability by route, using the existing finance data.
options.verdict: The question concerns last year's results, and the existing finance data answers it directly.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: A credit card issuer deployed a fraud model 18 months ago. Fraud losses have crept up over the past quarter although the model is unchanged. Payment patterns shifted after a higher tap-and-pay limit was introduced. The fraud manager asks the analyst what the original implementation plan should have included. The issuer's call centre moved to Adelaide. What was missing?
why: A model reflects the conditions it was trained in, and those conditions moved when the payment limit changed. Implementation should have set up monitoring, thresholds that trigger review and someone accountable for acting on them. A cleverer algorithm or more history at the start would still have aged, and freezing the business is not an option.

options.text: Monitoring of model performance, with triggers and an owner for review and retraining.
options.verdict: Performance drift was foreseeable, and the plan needed a way to detect and respond to it.

options.text: A more complex algorithm at the outset, so that the model stayed accurate for longer.
options.verdict: Complexity does not protect a model from changes in the behaviour it was trained on.

options.text: A requirement that payment limits remain fixed for as long as the model is in use.
options.verdict: The business cannot be held still to suit a model; the model has to keep up.

options.text: A larger training data set covering more years of historical card transactions.
options.verdict: More history could not have included payment patterns that had not yet occurred.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: Validating fuel-card data for a fleet efficiency study, the analyst finds 40 transactions out of 90,000 showing more than 400 litres in a single fill for light vehicles with 80-litre tanks. A colleague suggests deleting them as obvious errors; the fleet manager mentions that fuel theft has been suspected before. The study's sponsor is on leave until Monday. What is the best treatment of these records?
why: The values are impossible for the vehicles, but that makes them either recording errors or genuine transactions that were not for those vehicles. Which it is changes both the treatment and what the business needs to know. Validation means finding out from someone who knows, not deleting, smoothing or ignoring.

options.text: Replace them with the average fill for the vehicle class, so that the records are retained.
options.verdict: Substituting averages manufactures data and hides the anomaly from everyone.

options.text: Query them with the fleet manager first, since they may be errors or signs of misuse.
options.verdict: The right treatment depends on what the records are, and the fleet manager can help establish that.

options.text: Delete them, since values that exceed the tank capacity cannot be valid transactions.
options.verdict: Deletion assumes they are errors and discards what may be evidence of theft.

options.text: Keep them unchanged, since removing any observations would bias the efficiency results.
options.verdict: Leaving impossible fills in place would distort the efficiency figures they feed.

task: Document and Communicate Findings from Completed Analysis
trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: A data scientist's draft findings for a city parking study read: 'The gradient-boosted model achieved an AUC of 0.87; SHAP values indicate occupancy lag features dominate.' The audience is the councillors who will vote on changing parking fees. The analyst is asked to edit the document. The council chamber's audio system was upgraded last week. Which revision is most appropriate?
why: Councillors need to know what drives parking demand and what that means for the fee options in front of them. The draft is accurate and written for another data scientist. A glossary, an appendix or a feature chart keeps the same technical message; the revision required is a change of message, not more explanation of the jargon.

options.text: Add a glossary defining AUC, SHAP values and lag features for the councillors.
options.verdict: Defining the terms still leaves councillors to work out what the result means for fees.

options.text: Replace the sentence with a chart of the SHAP values for the top twenty features.
options.verdict: A feature-importance chart is the same technical message in another form.

options.text: State plainly what drives parking demand and what that means for the fee options.
options.verdict: This turns a technical result into the terms of the decision councillors have to make.

options.text: Keep the wording, but add the model's full parameter settings in an appendix.
options.verdict: More technical detail moves the document further from its audience.

trap: Misreading what an output or measure actually shows
stem: An insurer tests a fraud model on 10,000 past claims, of which 200 were fraudulent. The results are below. The data scientist reports 97.6% accuracy and the claims manager is delighted. Investigating a flagged claim costs $300. The insurer is moving offices in July. What should the analyst highlight?
why: Only 2% of claims are fraudulent, so a model that flagged nothing would score 98% accuracy. The figure that matters for the purpose is how much fraud is caught, and the model finds 60 of 200. Accuracy is high because legitimate claims dominate, not because the model does its job well.

options.text: The model is 97.6% accurate, so it is ready to replace manual selection of claims.
options.verdict: Flagging no claims at all would be 98% accurate, so this figure shows very little.

options.text: The model flags 100 legitimate claims, so it should be rejected as too costly to run.
options.verdict: False alarms have a cost, but that cost has to be weighed against fraud found, not judged alone.

options.text: The model was tested on too few claims for any conclusion to be drawn from the results.
options.verdict: Ten thousand claims with 200 frauds is enough to see that most fraud goes undetected.

options.text: The model misses 140 of the 200 fraudulent claims, so accuracy overstates its usefulness.
options.verdict: Catching 30% of fraud is the result that matters, and the accuracy figure conceals it.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A health fund wants to understand why members under 30 leave. The analyst can obtain exit-survey responses, which 8% of leavers complete, full membership and claims records, or call-centre notes. The marketing manager favours the exit survey because 'it tells us why in their own words'. The fund's app was redesigned in spring. Which consideration matters most in choosing the data sets?
why: With 92% of leavers not responding, the survey can only speak for the fund's leavers if respondents resemble non-respondents. If they differ, its vivid answers describe an unrepresentative few. That question of fit comes before any question of how the text would be processed or displayed.

options.text: Whether the exit survey's free-text answers can be processed with sentiment analysis tools.
options.verdict: How the text is processed matters only once the source is judged fit to use.

options.text: Whether the 8% who answered the exit survey resemble the leavers who did not respond.
options.verdict: If respondents differ from the other 92%, conclusions drawn from the survey will mislead.

options.text: Whether the claims records are stored in a format the visualisation tool can read directly.
options.verdict: File format is a practical matter and does not determine whether data fits the question.

options.text: Whether the app redesign changed the layout of the screens where the survey is offered.
options.verdict: The redesign is a planted detail and does not bear on which data sets suit the question.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A logistics group has 14 proposed analytics initiatives and funding for four. The chief data officer asks the analyst to recommend how to choose. The data science team prefers the projects using the newest techniques, and the most vocal executive wants his three funded. The group's strategy names on-time delivery and cost per parcel as its priorities. A staff picnic is planned for Friday. What should the selection be based on?
why: Analytics investment at organisation level is justified by its contribution to what the organisation is trying to achieve. The strategy names two priorities, which gives the test, tempered by whether each initiative can be delivered and at what cost. Novelty, seniority and even-handedness are all easier criteria that ignore value.

options.text: Expected contribution to the stated strategic priorities, weighed against feasibility.
options.verdict: The strategy states what matters, so initiatives are ranked by how much they advance it.

options.text: The technical novelty of each initiative, since new techniques build future capability.
options.verdict: Novelty serves the team's interests, not the group's stated priorities.

options.text: An even spread across departments, so that every part of the group receives a project.
options.verdict: Fairness between departments is not a measure of contribution to strategy.

options.text: The seniority of each initiative's sponsor, since executive support predicts delivery.
options.verdict: Sponsorship helps delivery, but it does not make an initiative valuable.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A university's student services team believes first-year attrition has 'got much worse' since orientation moved online, and asks the analyst to design a study of the online orientation's effect. Enrolment records show attrition of 14%, 15% and 14% in the three years before the change and 15% in the year after. The vice-chancellor recently launched a new strategic plan. What should the analyst conclude at this point?
why: The baseline shows attrition moving within its usual one-point range, so the perceived deterioration is not visible in the data. Before designing a study of a cause, the analyst needs to check with the team what they are seeing, since the problem as stated may not exist in this form.

options.text: Attrition data is unreliable and should be recollected before any conclusion is drawn.
options.verdict: Nothing in the scenario suggests the enrolment records are wrong; they simply disagree with the perception.

options.text: The strategic plan launch is the likelier cause and should replace orientation as the focus.
options.verdict: This swaps one unevidenced cause for another when no change has yet been shown.

options.text: The baseline does not show the change the team perceives, so the problem statement needs revisiting.
options.verdict: Attrition after the change sits inside the range of the three earlier years, so the premise needs checking first.

options.text: The one-point rise confirms the team's concern, so analysis of the online orientation should proceed.
options.verdict: A move from 14% to 15% matches earlier year-to-year variation and confirms nothing.

trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: An analysis of warehouse picking errors is complete. The findings must reach three groups: the executive team deciding on a $2 million automation investment, warehouse supervisors who will change shift practices, and the data team who will maintain the model. The analyst has one week. A colleague proposes a single 40-page report for everyone. The forklift fleet is being replaced. What should the communication plan specify?
why: The three groups will do three different things with the findings: decide on an investment, change daily practice and maintain a model. A communication plan matches what each receives to what each must do. One document for all serves none of them well, and a summary for executives alone abandons the other two.

options.text: A technical walkthrough of the model for all three groups, to build trust in the results.
options.verdict: Model detail suits the data team, but not executives or supervisors.

options.text: An executive summary only, since the investment decision is the most valuable outcome.
options.verdict: Supervisors and the data team also have to act, and a summary gives them nothing to act on.

options.text: A single comprehensive report, so that every group receives exactly the same information.
options.verdict: Identical information for all leaves each group to dig out the part that concerns them.

options.text: Content, depth and format for each group, matched to the decision or action each must take.
options.verdict: Each group uses the findings differently, so each needs its own message and level of detail.

trap: Skipping a stakeholder whose decision or data the work depends on
stem: A state transport agency is starting an analytics initiative on fare evasion. The sponsor, the revenue protection director, has supplied a list of questions. The analyst knows the results could change how authorised officers are rostered and where they are deployed, and that the officers' union recently negotiated a new agreement. The data team is keen to begin. Before the research questions are finalised, what should the analyst do?
why: The results will change rostering and deployment, so people beyond the sponsor will use or be affected by them. Their decisions and concerns shape which questions are worth asking. Feasibility checks and results briefings both come later than knowing who the work is for.

options.text: Identify who will use or be affected by the results and what decisions each needs supported.
options.verdict: Rostering and deployment decisions sit with people other than the sponsor, and their needs shape the questions.

options.text: Ask the data team to confirm which of the sponsor's questions the available data can answer.
options.verdict: A feasibility check is useful later, but it tests a question list that may be incomplete.

options.text: Schedule a results presentation for the officers' union so that findings are shared transparently.
options.verdict: Planning how to report results is premature when the questions themselves are not settled.

options.text: Finalise the sponsor's questions as written, since the sponsor funds the work and owns its outcome.
options.verdict: Sponsorship does not make the sponsor the only decision-maker the findings will reach.

trap: Ignoring data quality, bias, sampling or privacy because the result looks interesting
stem: A superannuation fund is studying why members consolidate their accounts elsewhere. Before analysis, the analyst profiles the extract below. The data scientist wants to begin modelling today and notes that the model handles missing values automatically. The fund's annual member statements go out next week. Which issue most needs resolving before analysis?

exhibit.title: Profile of member exit extract (86,000 records)
rows: Blank for all exits before July 2024

why: Exit reason is the field closest to the research question, it is blank for most records, and the blanks are not random: they cover every exit before a date. Automatic handling of missing values would treat a systematic gap as noise and bias any conclusion about why members leave.

options.text: Date of birth is incomplete for a small share of members and may distort age-based analysis.
options.verdict: A gap of 0.4% is worth noting but is too small to threaten the analysis.

options.text: Exit reason is missing for most records, in a pattern that depends on when the member left.
options.verdict: The gap is large, systematic and sits in the field the study most depends on.

options.text: Employer ID is missing for 3% of members, which prevents employer comparison for those rows.
options.verdict: This is a minor limitation next to a 59% gap in the key field.

options.text: Balance at exit is fully populated, which suggests values were defaulted and not captured.
options.verdict: Complete population is not in itself evidence of a fault, and nothing in the profile suggests one.

trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A credit union's lending team reports that personal loan approvals take nine days on average, against a competitor's advertised 'same day'. The head of lending asks the analyst to quantify how much faster approvals could be with automation. Last quarter the credit union also changed its logo. In discussion, the analyst learns that members rarely complain about speed, but 30% of approved applicants never draw down their loan. Which problem should the analyst propose framing the initiative around?
why: The evidence of lost value is the 30% of approved loans never drawn down; slow approval is an assumption, and members are not complaining about it. Speed may turn out to be a cause, but then it is a hypothesis to test under the draw-down problem, not the problem itself.

options.text: How far automation could shorten the nine-day approval time relative to the competitor's offer.
options.verdict: This frames the work around the stated request, although nothing shows that speed is what is costing the credit union.

options.text: Which approval steps contribute most to the nine-day elapsed time across the lending team.
options.verdict: Process analysis of approval time assumes the problem is speed before that has been established.

options.text: Why approved applicants do not draw down, since that is where the observed loss of value sits.
options.verdict: The draw-down gap is the measurable loss, and approval speed can be tested as one possible cause of it.

options.text: Whether the logo change has affected brand perception among recent personal loan applicants.
options.verdict: The logo change is a planted detail with no evidenced link to lending outcomes.

trap: Technically correct output for the wrong audience or the wrong decision
stem: An analyst must show a board how monthly electricity demand has changed over five years, including its seasonal peaks. Board members are not technical. A designer suggests a 3D pie chart for each year 'for impact'; a data scientist suggests a table of all 60 monthly values. The board papers are due on Wednesday. Which visual best meets the need?
why: The message is change over time with a repeating seasonal pattern, and a line chart shows both at a glance to a non-technical reader. Pie charts show shares of a whole, not movement through time, a 60-cell table leaves the pattern for the reader to find, and a scatter plot answers a question about temperature.

options.text: A scatter plot of demand against temperature, with a fitted regression line.
options.verdict: This shows a relationship with temperature, which is a different question from change over time.

options.text: A line chart of monthly demand over the five years, with the peaks labelled.
options.verdict: A line over time shows trend and seasonality directly, which is the message for the board.

options.text: A table listing all 60 monthly demand values, so that no detail is lost.
options.verdict: A table keeps the detail but makes readers find the pattern themselves.

options.text: A 3D pie chart for each year, showing each month's share of annual demand.
options.verdict: Pies show composition, not change through time, and 3D distorts the proportions.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Stopping at insight without recommendation, implementation or change
stem: Six months after a hotel group adopted analytics-based room pricing, revenue per room is up 6%. Revenue managers report that the tool's suggestions are poor during local events it does not know about, and two managers have gone back to spreadsheets. The project team has disbanded. The group has just opened a property in Hobart. What should the analyst recommend to sustain the change?
why: The benefit is real and already eroding, because nobody owns the tool and users' feedback has nowhere to go. Sustaining a change needs someone accountable and a route for what users learn to improve it. Declaring victory, enforcing use or starting over each leave that gap open.

options.text: Assign ownership for the tool and a route for managers' feedback to improve it.
options.verdict: Without an owner and a feedback path, known weaknesses stay unfixed and users drift away.

options.text: Require the two managers to return to the tool and stop using spreadsheets.
options.verdict: Enforcement does not fix the weakness that sent them back to spreadsheets.

options.text: Commission a new project to replace the pricing tool with a more advanced one.
options.verdict: The tool works; it lacks upkeep, not sophistication.

options.text: Declare the initiative complete, since the 6% revenue gain exceeded the target.
options.verdict: The gain is at risk while managers are abandoning the tool.

trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A council analyst has found that one contractor accounts for 60% of footpath repair rework. The finding is preliminary: two months of data remain to be validated. The procurement manager is negotiating that contractor's renewal this week and has not been told. The full report is scheduled for next month. The council's website is being redesigned. What should the analyst's communication approach be?
why: Communication is timed to the decisions it informs. A relevant finding exists, a decision it bears on is being made this week, and the decision-maker is unaware. Sharing it now with its caveats respects both the evidence and the timing. Waiting for the scheduled report delivers certainty after the contract is signed.

options.text: Send the contractor the data, so that they can respond before anything is reported.
options.verdict: The contractor is not the decision-maker, and this would cut across a live negotiation.

options.text: Hold the finding until validation is complete and the full report is issued next month.
options.verdict: By next month the renewal will be settled without the information.

options.text: Publish the finding on the intranet, so that all council staff can see the result.
options.verdict: Broadcasting an unvalidated finding about a named contractor is the wrong audience and channel.

options.text: Brief the procurement manager now on the preliminary finding and its caveats.
options.verdict: The renewal is being negotiated this week, and a caveated finding is more use than none.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: An analyst is evaluating three options for reducing stock-outs at an auto-parts distributor, using the results below. The supply chain director wants a recommendation. The capital budget available this year is $400,000. The distributor's website was redesigned in May. Which recommendation is best supported?
why: The recommendation has to fit the constraint and deliver value. B exceeds the budget. A and C both fit, but A returns $450,000 for $60,000 while C returns only $70,000 more for $320,000 more. A and C together cost $440,000, which is over budget, and their reductions cannot simply be added.

options.text: Options A and C together, since their combined reduction would exceed option B.
options.verdict: Together they cost $440,000, which exceeds the budget, and the two effects would overlap.

options.text: Option A, since it fits the budget and returns the most for its cost.
options.verdict: A is affordable and delivers most of the available benefit for a fraction of the outlay.

options.text: Option C, since it reduces stock-outs more than A and still fits the budget.
options.verdict: C fits, but it costs over six times as much as A for a small additional benefit.

options.text: Option B, since it delivers the largest reduction in stock-outs of the three.
options.verdict: B has the biggest effect, but at $900,000 it cannot be funded from a $400,000 budget.

trap: Misreading what an output or measure actually shows
stem: A safety analyst at a mining company reviews the incident figures below for the past year. The site manager at Ridge wants to report that Ridge is the safest site. The company's safety week is next month. Which conclusion do the figures support?
why: The sites worked very different numbers of hours, so raw counts mostly reflect exposure. The rate per 100,000 hours puts them on a common footing, and on that basis Ridge is the highest and Coast the lowest. Different hours are the reason to use a rate, not a reason the sites cannot be compared.

options.text: Valley is the least safe site, because it recorded the most incidents of the three.
options.verdict: Valley's count reflects its hours; its rate of 2.0 is below Ridge's 3.0.

options.text: The sites cannot be compared, because they worked different numbers of hours.
options.verdict: A rate exists to allow comparison when exposure differs.

options.text: Coast has the lowest incident rate once hours worked are taken into account.
options.verdict: At 1.5 incidents per 100,000 hours, Coast is lowest on the measure that allows comparison.

options.text: Ridge is the safest site, because it recorded the fewest incidents of the three.
options.verdict: Ridge has the fewest incidents because it worked the fewest hours; its rate is the highest.

trap: Choosing the most thorough option when the scenario constrains time or access
stem: A state health department must decide in six weeks whether to extend a telehealth pilot. Outcome data exists for 1,200 pilot patients, but no comparison group was set up. The epidemiology unit offers to design a randomised trial that would report in 14 months. The minister's office has asked for 'robust evidence'. The pilot's video platform was changed part-way through. How should the analyst plan the approach?
why: The decision is due in six weeks, so the approach has to produce the best available evidence in that time. A matched comparison from routine records gives the pilot outcomes a reference point, and stating the limits keeps the evidence honest. A trial reporting in 14 months cannot inform this decision.

options.text: Commission the randomised trial, since it is the design that provides the strongest causal evidence.
options.verdict: The trial is the most rigorous design, but it reports eight months after the decision is due.

options.text: Delay planning until the effect of the mid-pilot platform change has been separately evaluated.
options.verdict: The platform change is a limitation to note, not a reason to stall a time-bound decision.

options.text: Report the pilot patients' outcomes on their own, since no comparison group was established.
options.verdict: Outcomes with nothing to compare them against cannot show whether the pilot made a difference.

options.text: Compare pilot outcomes with matched patients from routine records, and state the evidence limits.
options.verdict: This gives the decision a comparison within the six weeks and is open about how far it can be relied on.

kaName: Guide Organization-level Strategy for Business Analytics
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A water utility has hired four data scientists. After a year they have built several accurate models, none of which is in use. Business units say the models 'answer questions nobody asked', and the data scientists say requirements are vague. The chief executive asks what capability is missing. The utility's billing cycle is moving to monthly. What should the analyst identify?
why: Both complaints describe the same gap from opposite sides: nobody is turning business problems into analytics questions and analytics results into decisions. That is a distinct capability, and without it technical talent produces unused output. More modellers or faster machines would produce more of it.

options.text: More data scientists, so that a larger number of models can be produced each year.
options.verdict: More models that nobody asked for would enlarge the problem.

options.text: People who translate business problems into analytics questions and results into action.
options.verdict: The missing link is between the business and the modellers, in both directions.

options.text: A faster computing platform, so that models can be trained and delivered more quickly.
options.verdict: Speed of delivery is not why the models go unused.

options.text: A requirement that business units accept and use any model that passes validation.
options.verdict: Mandating use of models that answer the wrong questions does not create value.

trap: Answering an easier or different question than the one asked
stem: A charity wants to tailor its appeals. It holds five years of donation history for 60,000 donors, but has no existing segments and no labelled outcome it wants to predict. The fundraising director asks for 'groups of donors who behave alike' so that three or four different appeals can be written. A board member suggests predicting who will donate next month. Which analysis should the plan lead with?
why: The director wants groups that are not yet known, and there is no outcome variable defining them. That is a segmentation task, which cluster analysis addresses. Predicting next month's donors answers the board member's question, a different one, and a test of letters presumes the segments already exist.

options.text: Cluster analysis on giving behaviour, to find groups of similar donors.
options.verdict: The need is for groups that are not predefined, which is what clustering is for.

options.text: An A/B test of two appeal letters on a random sample of donors.
options.verdict: Testing letters is a sensible later step once there are segments to write them for.

options.text: A classification model predicting whether each donor will give next month.
options.verdict: This answers the board member's question and produces a score, not the groups the director asked for.

options.text: A regression of annual donation amount on donor age and postcode.
options.verdict: Regression explains an amount and does not produce segments for writing appeals.

kaName: Use Results to Influence Business Decision Making
trap: Choosing a technically correct but not BEST answer
stem: A hospital is implementing a recommendation to add weekend discharge rounds, based on analysis showing they would free about 14 beds each Monday. The plan lists rosters, training and a start date. The nursing director asks how they will know it worked. Monday bed availability was measured as a baseline during the analysis. The hospital's helipad is being resurfaced. What should the analyst add to the plan?
why: The recommendation was justified by an expected outcome, and a baseline for that outcome already exists. The plan needs the measure, the comparison and a point at which it is reviewed, so the organisation learns whether the expected benefit arrived. A guarantee is not a measure, and staff sentiment is a different outcome.

options.text: A commitment that 14 beds will be free each Monday from the first week of operation.
options.verdict: A promise of the result is not a way of finding out whether it was achieved.

options.text: A staff satisfaction survey for the nurses and doctors working the weekend rounds.
options.verdict: Staff views are worth knowing, but they do not show whether beds were freed.

options.text: Measures and a review point comparing Monday bed availability with the baseline.
options.verdict: This tests the outcome the recommendation promised against the starting point already recorded.

options.text: A repeat of the original analysis using a further two years of discharge records.
options.verdict: Re-running the estimate says nothing about what the change did once introduced.

trap: Treating a stakeholder's stated want as the research question
stem: A forecasting team predicts next winter's emergency admissions at 14,200, with a plausible range of 12,900 to 15,600. The hospital's operations committee will use the forecast to set bed capacity. The committee chair has asked for 'just the number'. A junior analyst suggests giving 14,200 only, to avoid confusion. The hospital cafeteria is changing suppliers. How should the forecast be communicated?
why: Bed capacity has to cope with more than the central estimate, so the range is part of what the committee needs for its decision even though the chair asked for one figure. The analyst's job is to convey it in terms the committee can use. Hiding the uncertainty or handing over raw output both fail the decision.

options.text: Give the central figure with its range, and explain what the range means for capacity.
options.verdict: The capacity decision depends on how far admissions could exceed 14,200, so the range belongs in the message.

options.text: Give the full statistical output, so that the committee can interpret the intervals itself.
options.verdict: Raw output passes the interpretation to people who asked for a simple answer.

options.text: Give the upper figure of 15,600 only, so that capacity is planned on the safe side.
options.verdict: This makes the capacity decision on the committee's behalf and conceals the central estimate.

options.text: Give 14,200 only, as the chair requested, since a range would undermine confidence.
options.verdict: A single figure invites the committee to plan for a certainty the forecast does not offer.
